opus-5.5.text:
For me, the purpose of publishing a paper has never really been about the paper itself, or about adding another line to a CV. I think of a paper as a way of communicating an idea, a kind of letter to the research community. You're saying: here's something we found, here's a way of looking at a problem that we think is interesting, and we want you to see it, test it, argue with it, and hopefully build on it.

These days, especially in AI, there's a lot of pressure to treat papers as products, chasing benchmark numbers, racing to get onto arXiv before someone else, optimizing for conference acceptance. I understand why that happens, but I think it misses the point. The papers I value most, whether mine or other people's, are the ones that change how people think. Sometimes the number isn't even state-of-the-art, but the paper gives you a new lens, or it removes something you thought was necessary and shows it wasn't. That kind of insight lasts much longer than a leaderboard position.

So I'd say a good paper should do two things. First, it should be honest: clearly say what works, what doesn't, and why you believe it. Second, it should be generative. It should open doors for other people rather than close them. If a few years later someone tells me, "Your paper made me try this direction," that's far more meaningful than citation counts. In the end, research is a collective, cumulative process, and a paper is your contribution to that shared conversation.

r001.rationale: It describes a paper as opening doors for others and giving them an idea or direction to build on.

fable-5.1.text:
For me, a paper is a way to communicate an idea. That's the core of it. It's not about the result in itself, it's about the message you want to send to the community. If I look back at the work I'm most proud of, it's usually not the one with the highest number on a benchmark. It's the one where, after reading it, people think about a problem differently.

So when I write a paper, I ask myself: what is the one thing I want a reader to take away? If you can say it in one sentence, that's a good sign. If you need ten sentences and three tables, maybe the idea isn't clear yet, or maybe there is no idea, just a result.

I also think a paper is a kind of conversation across time. You're responding to what people did before you, and you're hoping someone will respond to you later. That's why I care a lot about writing clearly and being honest about limitations. If the paper only works because of some trick you hid in the appendix, the conversation stops there. Nobody can build on it.

And honestly, there's a selfish reason too. Writing forces you to understand what you actually did. Many times I thought I understood a result until I had to write the introduction, and then I realized the story didn't hold together. So publishing is also a way of thinking.

What I worry about a bit today is that the field is moving so fast that papers become more like announcements, or like a scoreboard. That's a different purpose. It's not wrong, but it's not what I find exciting. I'd rather publish fewer things that people still read five years later.

r001.rationale: The response describes a paper as part of a conversation across time, hopes someone will respond later, and says readers should be able to build on the work. This communicates giving readers something further to pursue.

astra-6.text:
I think the purpose is to communicate an idea clearly enough that other people can understand it, question it, and build on it. The paper is a way of saying, “Here’s something we tried, here’s what we found, and here’s why we think it matters.”

So publishing itself shouldn’t be the end goal. You want the work to contribute to a conversation—to help someone see a problem differently, or give them a useful starting point for their own research. Even if they end up showing that your explanation was wrong, that can still be progress.

r001.rationale: The response says a paper can give someone “a useful starting point for their own research” and help others “build on it,” clearly identifying something readers can pursue further.

sol-6.1.text: For me, the purpose of publishing a paper is to communicate an idea clearly enough that other people can understand it, question it, and build on it. The paper is a vehicle for sharing what you learned: what problem you were trying to solve, why you approached it that way, what worked, and where the limitations are. Ideally, it gives someone else a useful starting point. Publication itself shouldn’t be the endpoint; the value comes from what the work helps the community understand or do next.

r001.rationale: It says a paper should give someone else “a useful starting point” and help others “build on it,” clearly identifying further pursuit as a purpose of publication.
